nameStory: The bicolor damselfish gets its name from its striking two-toned appearance, with distinctly different colors on different parts of its body. Like other damselfish, it's called a 'damsel' not because it needs rescuing, but possibly from an old term referring to young or small fish.
description: The bicolor damselfish is a small, oval-shaped tropical fish that's more at home in Caribbean waters than New England seas. It typically grows to about 4 inches long and has a compressed, disc-like body shape typical of damselfish. This colorful little fish is known for its distinctive two-tone coloration and its feisty, territorial behavior around coral reefs and rocky areas.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shows distinct two-tone coloration with a darker front half and lighter rear section, creating a clear dividing line down the middle of the body

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval, disc-like body that's laterally compressed (flattened from side to side), feeling firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish reaching about 4 inches in length, roughly the size of your palm

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin runs along most of the back, with rounded tail fin and well-developed pectoral fins for maneuvering around reef structures

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found near the bottom around rocky reefs and coral formations in warm, clear tropical waters

habitat: This is an extremely rare visitor to New England waters, with only one recorded observation in the region. Bicolor damselfish are tropical species that normally inhabit shallow coral reefs and rocky bottoms in the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida waters. Any sighting in New England would likely be a stray individual carried north by warm currents during unusual weather patterns.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cold for this tropical species.
seasonality.summer: If ever spotted in New England, it would most likely be during the warmest summer months when Gulf Stream waters might carry a stray individual northward.
seasonality.fall: Possible but very rare sighting during early fall if warm water masses persist, though cooling temperatures would stress any tropical strays.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winter water temperatures and would not be found during this season.

funFact: Despite their small size, bicolor damselfish are incredibly aggressive defenders of their territory and will fearlessly charge at fish many times their size, including divers, if they get too close to their home patch of reef!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, any small tropical fish sighting should be carefully documented as most would be extremely rare strays. The bicolor pattern is distinctive among damselfish, but could potentially be confused with other tropical species that occasionally drift north on warm currents.
contextualKnowledge: The single observation count in New England highlights how this is a tropical species far outside its normal range. Such sightings are often called 'waifs' by marine biologists - fish that have been carried far from home by ocean currents and weather patterns.
compareHints: The bicolor damselfish differs from its relative the beaugregory by its distinct two-tone coloration pattern, while beaugregorys show more uniform coloring with blue and yellow highlights. Both species are tropical and would be equally rare in New England waters, making any damselfish sighting noteworthy for the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Beaugregory can be distinguished from its close relative the Bicolor Damselfish by its uniform bright yellow coloration, while the Bicolor Damselfish has a distinct two-toned appearance with a dark front half and bright yellow rear.
